errors.english: It is illogical for anything to arise without a cause, just as the sky cannot be a cause for production.
errors.why: The Tibetan says arising without a cause is untenable, like space and the like (which do not arise); nothing about the sky being a cause.

fix.find: It is illogical for anything to arise without a cause, just as the sky cannot be a cause for production.
fix.replace: For it is untenable that they arise without a cause, as space and the like [would then be].

errors.english: since neither is ultimately real, the aggregates of cyclic existence are actually inherently blissful
errors.why: The opponent says suffering, being from habituation, is not ultimate, therefore the aggregates are bliss; 'neither' makes the argument incoherent.

errors.english: In the absence of true pleasure, one might perceive something as pleasurable that is actually neither pleasure nor pain.
errors.why: The Tibetan says that, in the absence of that [fear-habituation], the notion of pleasure arises toward that very suffering or toward what is neither; 'that very suffering' is dropped and the absence misidentified as of pleasure.

fix.find: In the absence of true pleasure, one might perceive something as pleasurable that is actually neither pleasure nor pain.
fix.replace: Therefore, in its absence, the notion of pleasure arises toward that very suffering, or toward what is neither pleasure nor pain.

note: Follows the argument in outline but garbles the causelessness rebuttal and the closing point about suffering being taken as pleasure.

errors.english: Only stay until it is born,
errors.why: The verse describes the fawn just born, which she will lick and suckle; it is not an imperative to stay.

errors.english: The affection of the holy increases greatly even toward those in misery who are strangers
errors.why: The closing passage from 'bu la gdung ba'i ri dags mo' onward is verse (with shad-delimited lines) but is rendered as continuous prose.

note: Faithful narrative and dialogue; minor misconstrual in the doe's verse and verse turned to prose at the end.

errors.why: khyad par med pa mtshungs pa is the Nyāya jāti aviśeṣasama.

errors.english: Because the phrase "would absurdly result in non-difference" has multiple meanings
errors.why: It is the verb 'byed pa' that has many meanings, here taken in the sense of consequence, not the whole phrase.

note: Generally accurate rendering of a dense jāti discussion; one wrong Sanskrit label.
A faithful rendering of the latrine rules, root sūtra and gloss kept distinct enough.

errors.why: yan lag mchog renders uttamāṅga, 'head', not 'supreme limbs'.

errors.english: lotuses arose, calling out to the swarms of six-legged bees
errors.why: The lotuses' golden pericarp with filaments and anthers, on this side, is not rendered.

note: Readable verse rendering with Sanskrit kept in notes; one technical body term wrong.

errors.english: The opponent says: "From the familiarity of others," and so forth.
errors.why: gzhan gyi marks the words as the opponent's ('from familiarity'), not familiarity belonging to others.

fix.find: The opponent says: "From the familiarity of others," and so forth.
fix.replace: The opponent says: "From familiarity," and so forth.

errors.english: the unstable object of appropriation itself perishes
errors.why: nye bar len pa here is the material cause (upādāna): the object whose material cause is unstable perishes.

errors.english: Others, thinking it is impossible to deny the experienced object, show the sequence of engaging with experience
errors.why: It is the author who, anticipating others' doubt, shows the sequence with 'the very seeing of that'; others do not show it.

note: Dialectical structure mostly clear, but the attribution of several moves is muddled.

errors.english: Whatever touches exceptionally pure silk, sweet-scented flowers, honey, or saffron instantly becomes foul.
errors.why: It is the pure silk, flowers, honey and saffron that instantly become impure wherever they touch the body.

fix.find: Whatever touches exceptionally pure silk, sweet-scented flowers, honey, or saffron instantly becomes foul.
fix.replace: Exceptionally pure silk, sweet-scented flowers, honey, or saffron instantly become foul wherever they touch it.

errors.english: and place my trust in truth

note: Vivid and mostly faithful rendering of the meditation on the body; one inverted image.

errors.english: Consequently, how can the awareness of the past and so forth be a direct perception…
errors.why: The sentence continues on the next side with a reason clause, so it explains how the cognition of the past is perception rather than asking a doubting question.

note: Accurate on the argument about sense-functioning known by inference and yogic perception.
Faithful word-gloss commentary on the dhyāna similes, with sound terminology.

errors.english: Therefore, one might ask: "Was it not done by oneself out of one's own desire?"
errors.why: The commentator concludes that the fourfold examination is drawn from the text and is not his own arbitrary arrangement; it is not an opponent's question.

errors.english: such as a continuous stream of provisions
errors.why: rgyun here refers to the stream/water channel case of theft cited just before, not a stream of provisions.

note: Vinaya theft analysis rendered soundly, with pārājika correctly glossed.
